answer: Readers call an API server, which talks to the production MongoDB (plus, later, a dashboard tool). Readers never touch the database; they reach it only through the API. The page does not spell out why beyond that.

A dashboard tool such as Grafana or Metabase fires its queries straight at production; usually the first step after that is to point it at a read replica so heavy queries don't slow the app. Works up to roughly 10k-50k users.
Production holds everyone's personal data (PII), so handing it even read-only is risky; also production is MongoDB while analysts (and warehouses) work in SQL; heavy queries can slow the app.

When a blog is published the API server writes MongoDB and publishes a blog_published event (carrying the id) to Kafka; consumers read the events and write rows into an analytics MySQL that the insights team queries.

1) changes with no event at all (views++, a likes aggregation job that bypasses the API); 2) events too thin: they lack data so the consumer must fetch the rest from the DB (load) or messages become large; 3) dual write: API saves the row then crashes before publishing; 4) a new table whose event nobody remembered to add. None raises an error; the copy silently drifts.
Change Data Capture: any change in the data is captured; rather than trusting events from the API server, read changes from the actual source of truth, the database itself (its log).
Debezium and Airbyte; Airbyte was found the easier to set up.

It reads the database's change log (MySQL binlog, Postgres WAL via logical decoding, MongoDB oplog via change streams), keeping a checkpoint; if the store has no change log (e.g. Elasticsearch) it can only iterate/scan the table rows again and again (needs a last_updated column; misses deletes between scans). It starts with a snapshot.

In a hash table in memory: keys in an array, each with a pointer to where its value is stored.

Wrap each value in a small struct (MyValue) with a void* pointer to the value and a type field; before running a command, get the value, read its type, check the type supports the operation, then cast and run.
Putting the type in the key (set:myset) means every lookup must parse it; a wrapper per value also has room to grow for more metadata (LRU bits, expiry).
4 bits (16 types, there are only 5-10). Principle: in memory, be careful with every byte and every bit, because RAM is expensive and the cost multiplies by millions of keys.
malloc returns NULL (a careful program checks and refuses the write), or on Linux the OOM killer ends the process.
Cap its own memory so it never reaches the limit, and therefore know how much memory it uses; evict or refuse writes at the cap.
The kernel knows the number so every check is a system call; the cache needs it on every write, and a syscall each time would slow it down.
sizeof measures only the 16-byte wrapper (pointer + type); the value it points to (e.g. a 1 MB Bloom filter) is a separate allocation the counter never sees.
malloc takes a number of bytes and returns an address from the process heap (asking the OS for more when low); free gives a block back, marking it reusable.
Everything stored (wrappers, Bloom filters, sets, list nodes) is allocated by the same malloc and released by the same free, so counting there includes the values themselves.
zmalloc(b) { while total_size + b > maxmemory -> evict; o = malloc(b); total_size += b; return o; } (zfree subtracts).
With malloc at e.g. 50,000 places in a codebase, forgetting one makes the count wrong for good; the wrapper does it in one place.
1 GB cap on a 32 GB machine (maxmemory). Hard/soft is not labelled; in our design it's checked before every allocation (a hard cap); Redis checks once per command.
Inside zmalloc: before allocating, if total_size + b would pass the cap, evict keys (then allocate). Redis does it once per command before executing.
LRU: least recently used, evicts the key used longest ago. LFU: least frequently used, counts accesses and evicts the one used least.
In each key's object header (the value wrapper), 24 bits sharing one 32-bit word with 4-bit type and 4-bit encoding: one integer of metadata per key.
Hash map + doubly linked list: map stores each key's node; on access unlink and move node to head in O(1); evict from the tail.
Three pointers (next, prev, value) = 12 bytes with 4-byte pointers, 24 with 8-byte; the example a -> 2 is 5 bytes of data: overhead exceeds data.
Fine where memory is not the constraint; in a cache every pointer is room another key could use.
Random eviction: the most memory-efficient, no per-key bookkeeping, fast.
May evict a key that should have stayed (popular key -> one miss), but needs no bookkeeping so more keys fit and eviction is fast; not optimal.
The cache took in many more keys with only a very small rise in miss ratio; net positive.

a=10, both add 1: each writes 'a = 11 where a = 10'; via CAS, thread 1 succeeds, thread 2 finds 11, fails, re-reads and retries CAS(11->12): a = 12. Implemented with the CPU compare-and-swap instruction (sync/atomic, std::atomic).
The hardware does the compare and write as one indivisible operation every core sees whole; nothing can slip in between.
